note: Rabbi Meir recalled that while studying with Rabbi Akiva he used to add iron sulfate to the ink he wrote Torah scrolls with, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing. When he came to study with Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yishmael asked his trade, and on hearing he was a scribe warned him to be careful, since leaving out or adding a single letter could destroy the whole world. Rabbi Meir replied that he put iron sulfate into his ink. Rabbi Yishmael objected: the Torah says the curses of the sota scroll are to be blotted out, so the writing must be erasable.
why: The mishna has just described the woman suspected of adultery drinking the water into which the scroll's curses are blotted; the Gemara opens with this exchange over ink that cannot be erased, then raises a version with the teachers reversed.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe of Torah scrolls who tells of studying with two teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers, who did not object to his ink.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Another teacher of Rabbi Meir, who warned him about his work and his ink.

terms.meaning: A substance added to ink to make the writing permanent so it cannot be washed off.
A wife suspected of adultery. In the Temple rite, curses were written on a scroll and dissolved in water that she drank.
One who writes Torah scrolls and other sacred texts by hand, where every letter must be exact.

note: Yohanan the High Priest sent messengers throughout the Land of Israel and found that people set aside only the main priestly gift from their produce, while some gave the first and second tithes and some did not. He told them that eating produce without the tithe of the tithe taken, or untithed produce, carries a penalty of death at the hand of Heaven, just as with the main gift. He then made an ordinance: anyone who buys produce from an unlearned person must set aside the first and second tithes himself. The tithe of the tithe goes to a priest and the second tithe is eaten in Jerusalem, but the Levite and the poor cannot demand their shares without proof.
why: The mishna says Yohanan the High Priest abolished the declaration of tithes; the Gemara had explained that people gave the tithe to priests rather than Levites, and this account, showing many did not tithe at all, challenges that, leading to the answer that he made two separate ordinances.

people.name: Yohanan the High Priest
people.about: He investigated tithing across the land and instituted the ordinance on doubtfully tithed produce.

terms.meaning: The main gift from a harvest that must be given to a priest before the produce may be eaten.
Tenths of produce: the first tithe goes to the Levites, who give a tenth of it to priests; the second tithe is eaten by its owner in Jerusalem; the poor man's tithe goes to the poor.
An unlearned person, who could not be trusted to have set aside the required tithes.
Produce bought from someone who may not have tithed it; Yohanan's decree requires the buyer to tithe it.
